r303 commit log:
Fix for problem with electron transport
- Provide a variant of dagmc_chkcel that behaves correctly when the
  test point is known to be at zero distance from a surface crossing.
  This variant operates only in terms of the direction of the particle.
- Use this variant at the appropriate place in echkcl.  This is a
  candidate fix for ticket 446.  I'm not certain it's the _best_
  fix, but it's worth testing.
- Get rid of a lot of unused parameters in dagmcchkcel_
- Document dagmc_chkcel_\* functions
- Add a lot more tracing calls when TRACE_DAGMC_CALLS macro is defined.

r307 commit log:
wo bug workarounds for electron transport, both hacky:
- Only treat a call to track() as a streaming event if it is the first
  call to track() since the last call to newcel()
  (i.e., if it is the first call since a surface was traversed).
  If it's not the first such call, assume the particle didn't make
  it to the surface after all, and call rollback_last_intersection()
  on the ray history.
  
  What it fixes: situations where an electron advances part of the way
  along a particle track, then has some kind of event, then proceeds
  _along the same ray_ with a second call to track().  We want such
  a call to return the same intersection as the first call.
  
  Why it's a hack: this isn't the right way to tell whether or not
  to roll back the ray history.  The right way will be to detect all
  cases in MCNP where a particle's location is updated within its
  cell without reaching a surface or changing direction, and calling
  the rollback function in those cases.
- Add a dagmc_particle_terminate() function and call it when particles
  die.  This function clears the ray history.  It is a step towards a
  more comprehensive understanding of particle events within the dagmc
  glue code.  (In the long run, we want to avoid having to infer such
  events from changes in program globals like xyz and nps.)
  
  Also call this function from getpar, which restores particle state from
  a temporary cache location that's distinct from the particle bank.
  
  What it fixes: situations where a particle spawns a new particle
  and state is temporarily stored in the savpar/getpar cache, leading
  dagmc to detect a streaming event when one should not occur.
  
  Why it's a hack: A call to getpar does not actually represent a
  particle termination, and should not necessarily lead to a discarding
  of the entire particle history.  (I don't think discarding the
  history in this situation will ever lead to incorrect computation,
  so this workaround should be conservative.)
  This fix should be considered a short-term workaround while I figure
  out how the savepar/getpar cache should be integrated with the bank
  of ray histories.  See notes on ticket #445.

This update requires MOAB r5044.

2011-Aug-15 17:38:44 by sjackson:

sourcb.F90 is a maintainer's nightmare.  (Out of 650 lines, 49 lines contain goto statements, 28 lines are numeric labels, and and 26 lines contain cycle statements.  Sigh.)

In the tests I'm doing, setting the dagmc check_src_cell=off card in an input file does not actually disable chkcel calls for newly born particles.  This issue is observed in ticket 440.  Fixing this feature is probably the first issue to address in dealing with sourcb.F90.  Ticket 265 rightly observes "I think the chkcel call in sourcb.f90 around line 522 needs circumvented."  There is code in sourcb.F90 that attempts to implement the dagmc source cell optimization, but I am doubtful whether this implementation was ever completely right, at least for most cases.  I'd be curious to see the input files for any test cases where the source cell optimization was believed to have worked correctly.

_2011-Aug-16 16:57:12 by sjackson:

I made two changes in r324 to attempt to fix support for check_src_cell=off.
- **(A)** Add code at line 519 that skips a call to chkcel if DAGMC is enabled and user has called for this optimization.
- **(B)** Remove code around line 570 that skips a call to chkcel and related bookkeeping under the comment heading default for cel: find the cell that contains xyz.

These changes are sufficient to allow the unit test given in ticket 449 to behave as intended (particles spawned in the wrong cell get lost when the optimization is applied).

I'm not sure part **(B)** should ever have been implemented.  The only behavioral difference I observed is that it causes MCNP5 to crash if =check_src_cell=off= is specified and the user forgets to add a =CEL= entry to the =SDEF= card.  I think this code segment may only have executed when the =CEL= entry is not given on the =SDEF= card.  But I am not sure, given the complexity of sourcb.

I've changed the glue code to print a warning on stdout that the source cell optimization is experimental.  I'm not sure r324 is sufficient or correct in all cases.  I am also hesitant to continue spending time on making this optimization work correctly, because its benefit is often minor: it saves one call to =chkcel= per particle history, resulting in a savings of one ray-fire per history.

_2011-Aug-04 12:40:33 by sjackson:_

MCNP5 requires its OpenMP compiler to support both the THREADPRIVATE and EQUIVALENCE attributes for the same variable.  Our current fortran compiler (gfortran 4.3.2) does not.  It produces errors such as:

  Error: EQUIVALENCE attribute conflicts with THREADPRIVATE attribute in 'xxx' at (1)

(=xxx= being one of the many variables that participates in EQUIVALENCE statements.)

A gfortran bug was filed against this issue in 2009 [here](http://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=38979).  It does not appear to have been fixed yet, although a patch does exist that allows the code to compile.  We could apply this patch if we were willing to build a custom version of gfortran.  The alternative is to work with a different compiler (which would probably entail using a different compiler system for the dag-mcnp5 glue code and MOAB, and possibly sorting out a different scheme for calling C functions from Fortran).

_2011-Aug-04 12:46:42 by sjackson:_

Once we have compiler support for building OpenMP MCNP5, it remains to be determined whether MOAB's DagMC object can support multithreaded access.  In principle, it should, since the queries made by MCNP5 are theoretically read-only.  TimTautges mentioned that MOAB does some internal caching to speed up queries, and this caching may not be thread-safe.  He thought it wouldn't be terribly difficult to work around this, and it might even work correctly (possibly slowly) without any intervention.

The current version of the dag-mcnp5 glue code is **not** thread-safe: it uses a handful of static variables that would need to become thread-local.  Need to investigate the best way to do this-- whether through OpenMP directives or pthread calls or, on the right compiler, the =__thread= keyword.  (Or, on a very modern compiler supporting c++0x, the =thread_local= keyword.)

_2011-Aug-04 13:17:26 by sjackson:_

There's a pgf90 installation at /afs/engr.wisc.edu/apps/bin/pgf90.  It _does_ compile mcnp5 with OpenMP enabled, however, it stubbornly refuses to generate 64-bit code, and in 32-bit mode I can't coax it to get past the linking step when building dagmc.   (It has trouble finding a 32-bit =crtbegin.o=, probably a gcc configuration issue, probably not the only issue we'd run into following this path.  Anyway, we'd want our OpenMP version to be 64-bit, so fixing the 32-bit build isn't the right path.)

@julry asked:

Before I test the script to "make gh-pages", do I modify+commit a *.rst file, or do I modify+commit+push?   E.g. I found a small syntax error in DAGMC/doc-src/source/doc/usrersguide/workflow.rst and made a change on my local branch.  I'm thinking I have to push first, or I'll lose the changes when I do a checkout, right?

reply:

You need to modify+commit in the master branch, but you should not need to push the master branch.  You're best to do that AFTER you determine that the change is correctly processed by Sphinx.  (Of course, do remember to fetch/merge the master branch from github first so as to avoid undoing any changes made by others.) Remember to push the master branch after you are sure that it works.

2.  I got errors after the push:

error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/svalinn/DAGMC.git'
Maybe these errors are due to the untracked .gitignore and FluDAG/\* files on the gh-pages branch
3.  I see the change in the github file, but I don't see it on http://svalinn.github.com/DAGMC/doc/usersguide/workflow.html

Regarding (1): yes - you will want to have your working repo in a committed state otherwise when you try to checkout another branch, it will complain.  "git reset HEAD" will delete/remove changes (nominally) while "git stash" will tuck those changes away to be retrieved at another time.

Regarding (2): If you error message is faithful (cut & paste) it looks like you tried to push the wrong branch:  the error message refers to 'gh-page' (singular) vs 'gh-pages' (plural)

Regarding (3): You probably see your changes to the source in the master branch because those came before any of these steps anyway.

Yes, that is the same issue I had with the simple cylinder problem as well.  I looked back at my emails from Steve when I asked about it and he said that this is because the conformal logic requires an exact match between the geometry and mesh.  With curved surfaces this is not always the case, so these epsilon errors pop up.  If you refine the mesh, the errors get smaller as the two surfaces get closer to one another.  To resolve this for the cylinder testing problem, we had to use the dagmc pre-processing tool to replace the geometric surface with the mesh.

Found an old bug ticket from Steve in my emails that explains this error a bit more...

"Track length mesh tallies run into numerical issues when the tetrahedral tally mesh has a boundary that exactly coincides with the triangular facets in DagMC. The tally code is not currently aware of surface crossings, but when tally tracks stop and start exactly on tally boundaries (e.g. at surface crossings), the tally tracking code can get confused. It is not very predictable whether a point exactly on a triangle boundary will appear to be inside or outside the associated tetrahedron.

I have committed a test case ("metroid") to the meshtal branch of DAG-MCNP that illustrates this issue, and am working towards a fix."

A followup to the bug ticket from Steve...

"I know a way for the mesh tally code to monitor MCNP's notion of the current cell (by keeping track of MCNP's =icl= global). If this variable changes between two calls to =dagmc_fmesh_score=, then a surface crossing has occurred.

I propose to add a flag to the track length mesh tally input card, specifying that the tally is fully conformal to DagMC's surface geometry. When this flag is set, the tally code can monitor the =icl= variable to detect surface crossings, and use special logic to avoid numerical problems for track segments that touch the surface boundaries. In effect, ray firing at the tally boundaries can be skipped, because DagMC has already done those calculations. This may lead naturally towards a solution where fully conformal mesh tallies specify the MCNP cell(s) to which they conform."

Ran another test case using spherical geometry, and this does not have the negative track warnings without the conformal flag (although not surprisingly it does have the epsilon warning with the conformal flag).  So it appears as though only meshes with "flat" surfaces such as the rectangular prism and the cylinder cause the problem since they are exactly conformal to the geometry with the precision set by the track length mesh tally.  This may help to explain why you see repeated tracks with the same negative values.

Here are the instructions that Steve gave me for setting up conformal track length tallies that require geometric surfaces being replaced with mesh surfaces in order for the conformal logic to work properly:

1) Create your geometry CAD file, geometry.sat.

2) Load geometry.sat into cubit (be sure attributes are enabled with a command like `set attrib on` before loading).  Mesh whatever volume(s) you care about-- for this example we'll use volume 2.  Save only the meshed volumes as a .cub file with the following cubit command: `export cubit 'mesh.cub' vol 2` .  This will give you mesh.cub with surface numbers identical to geometry.sat.

3) `mbconvert mesh.cub mesh.h5m`

4) Run `dagmc_preproc -v --ftol [tolerance] -m mesh.h5m -o output.h5m geometry.sat`.  The options are as follows:
- -v -- verbose output, which may be useful to follow the program's progress.
- --ftol [tolerance] -- this is optional, and lets you specify a faceting tolerance like you would on a dag-mcnp5 command line.  The tolerance will not apply to the surfaces that are replaced with mesh surfaces.
- -m mesh.h5m -- specifies the alternative mesh file.  Surfaces in this file will replace identically-numbered surfaces from geometry.sat
- -o output.h5m -- specify an output file name.
- geometry.sat -- the required input argument.

5) Create a dag-mcnp5 problem using output.h5m as the gcad file on the dag-mcnp5 command line.  Set up a conformal mesh tally using mesh.h5m as the input mesh, and add conformal=2 to the FC card.

For some added background information, often in complex geometries such as seen with ITER, one does not want to mesh an entire volume since the mesh element count will get very high.  Thus I often only mesh a portion of a geometry volume and so setting conformal=2 does not seem appropriate.  Of course I can go back and modify the original geometry and create a volume in the place where I want a mesh tally, but in complex geometries such as seen with ITER, this can be very time consuming and problematic.  So the bottom line is, I just want the option where the mesh tally is not necessarily conformal to the geometry to work.

The master version of MeshTally currently has fairly minimal interaction with actual MOAB methods.  It uses the moab::Range only to determine what index value to use with the tally data arrays for a given entity handle, and sets up moab::Tag handles for tagging the results corresponding to each energy bin to the output mesh.  Keeping MOAB would probably mean that more common functionality from the two derived classes could be brought up to the MeshTally level to remove some of the redundancy in the code.

The other option that I was considering was to make a new abstract class called MeshData that would be responsible for all interactions with the tally points and handle input/output operations for these points.  Derived classes could either use MOAB or another mesh representation for this as long as the required set of functions were implemented from MeshData.  All the MeshTally base class really cares about is what index to use for storing the tally data for each tally point so it would just refer to some MeshData object for that purpose.

The hardest part with this second option would be then removing the MOAB dependency from the derived mesh tally classes since they are not set up exactly the same way and use different methods from MOAB.  This may mean it makes more sense and is easier to keep the MOAB dependency for this reason alone.  Thoughts?

My main thought is that MOAB is essentially a "MeshData" class already.  Why reinvent the wheel?  Hooking up codes with different native mesh formats might be a matter of moving all the data into MOAB at setup and writing it all back out of MOAB at shutdown, and then do everything in MOAB during the simulation.

The MeshData concept is a little different from directly using MOAB because it would only include purely virtual functions needed for mesh tally applications, which makes the MeshTally base class more general and leaves it up to the derived classes to determine what mesh representation to use.  On the other hand, we could always override the MOAB behavior in the derived classes as well so it is really more of a style issue than an implementation issue.  For now, I will focus on removing the MCNP dependency.

Upon further investigation of the MCNP mesh tally code, the dagmc_mesh_score function is only called from within the DAGMC advanced mesh tally code.  Other than for the special multiplier case that tallies the number of tracks, this function currently always computes:

```
score = track_length * particle_weight * tally_multipliers
```

We could just divide out the track_length part, but what I would prefer to do is to change this function so that it just returns only the tally_multipliers part (this would include the energy and dosef multipliers if requested).  Then I would pass both the particle_weight and tally_multipliers to the individual mesh tally implementations for computing the final scores.  All of the mesh tally implementations can then be generalized to the following:

```
final_score = score * particle_weight * tally_multipliers
```

The only difference between the different mesh tally implementations would be how score is computed.  I think that this makes the implementation cleaner and easier to understand outside of MCNP.
Many improvements remain, but this task is essentially complete.  Remaining test issues should specify what needs to be tested.

I suppose we could always pass through a track length of d=1 as well since that would not change the results that were reported back by MCNP.  I already do this for KDE track length tallies.  However, since this function is only used by the DAGMC advanced mesh tally code, it makes more sense to me to just change it so that it works for general mesh tally implementations instead.

The new compute_score function will now work for both collision and track-based events so that only one function is needed for the public interface instead of two separate implementations.  First, a check is made to ensure that the event type to be scored is valid for the specific KDE tally that was created.  Then a neighborhood region is constructed and all the calculation points for the tally event are determined.  Next, the tally weighting factor is computed once (this step is a little bit different for collision and sub-track tallies).  Finally, the set of calculation points is processed to compute the actual scores using the estimator that is associated with the type of KDE tally that was created.  There are three different estimator functions now that were brought over to KDEMeshTally from KDECollision and KDETrack: integral_track_estimator, sub_track_estimator, and collision_estimator.

Note that all the functionality that used to exist within KDECollision and KDETrack that is still needed has been moved to either KDEMeshTally, KDENeighborhood or TallyEvent.  Thus, these old classes have been removed.  I am putting this issue into review status.

The current tetmesh tally in DAGMC has one method for computing the score for a single track segment and then another method at the end of history.  However, the end_history method just adds the temporary tally data to the total tally data and error arrays.  You could probably implement it in Fluka at every track segment or wait until the end of history if you have a record of all the track data for that history, as the MeshTally implementation doesn't care when you call the compute_score method as  long as it is done before you call the end_history method.  However, I would think that using mgdraw.f would be the easiest option to implement.

As for the refactoring status, I am planning on changing the interface to MeshTally in the near future to make it easier to hook up into other physics codes.  Once this interface is finished you will be able to start implementing the tetmesh scoring for Fluka, as the rest of the code will be encapsulated.

I think that the trickiest part of this script will be how to determine external boundary surfaces.  We may need to use MOAB instead of PyTAPS, since I cannot see any part of PyTAPS that allows us to get the boundaries of the mesh.  Does MOAB have this capability?

Thank you for the tip Andy, I will check out MBSkinner.  Actually I need external boundaries of the geometry itself, since if the mesh is completely inside the geometry (i.e. further than one bandwidth from those external boundaries) the boundary correction is not needed.

Since the boundary kernel changes with distance from the external boundary, and we are working in 3D, then we will also need to be able to tag the distance from the point to each of the lower and upper boundaries in each dimension.  Therefore, I propose that we add two 3D tags as follows:
- lower_bound_distance(x, y, z)
- upper_bound_distance(x, y, z)

We will be calculating this information in the script for every mesh node, so may as well store it in a tag for every mesh node.  Then, inside the KDEMeshTally code we can test if these distances are less than or greater than the bandwidth in each dimension if boundary correction has been requested by the user.  Otherwise we'd just ignore these tags.

Originally I was thinking that we could just tag the mesh nodes as boundary points, but this will not be enough information on its own to use the boundary kernel evaluate method in 3D.  We could still add an integer-based tag that states how many dimensions need the boundary correction.  Most of the mesh nodes will not be boundary points, or will only need correction in one dimension, so this could reduce the number of inequalities that are tested during run time per node.

Another option is to add only two tags as follows:
- MB_TYPE_INTEGER: BOUNDARY(b, x, y, z) where b=1 means it is a boundary point, b=0 means it is a normal point; and x, y, & z indicate lower boundary(=0), upper boundary(=1) or neither boundary (=-1) in each dimension
- MB_TYPE_DOUBLE: DISTANCE_TO_BOUNDARY(x, y, z): represents distance to the x, y, or z boundary side defined in the boundary tag

Using this tag setup means that when we call the boundary evaluate method we can just pass the distance and boundary side variables directly from the tag data without having to use if-else statements depending on whether it is a lower or upper boundary.

1) fire a ray from the start point and determine the distance to all tet faces that we intersect, by doing so record the handle to the nodes that belong to that tet

  3) Take the vertex data and determine the tet centroid
-  If inside a tet then the score is taken from the distance vector for that tet
-  If not inside then this corresponds to a non score
-  If we scored for that tet add that tracklength score to the array

If it just passed an incremental score, then how would the mesh tally know where to put that score?  It has to identify the energy bin somehow, even if it is just an array index passed with the score.  We currently use energy bin boundaries to set up tag names on the mesh during initialization to identify different energy bins.  However, in the old MeshTally code we were relying on MCNP to give us the energy bin with every tally event, even though we were also asking for the particle energy and doing nothing with it.

Thats the exact point, in the case of Fluka there will only be a single bin to put it in, i.e. what ever quantity is being scored, there is no energy dimension to fluka mesh tallies, just the quantity being scored. e.g. dose, heat, flux, activity  etc.

That shouldn't be a problem, since if there is only one energy bin then we don't need to search at all and will just return a value of 0 for the index.  The tally data is stored in an array that is sized by the number of energy bins, and 1 energy group is a completely valid option.  It was originally implemented as a single energy group, and multiple groups were added later on.

Although this may be another good reason for moving the energy bin boundaries to the tally options instead of as a required variable.  It is simple enough to set up a single energy group with the current implementation, but shouldn't be necessary if energy is not tracked at all.

One more thing we need to fix here is how each tally responds to the event type that has been set.  Right now we are just exiting if an incorrect event type is given to the concrete mesh tally implementations.  However, since we update all the tallies with each tally event and they may get invalid event types, we will need to account for that in the compute_score methods.

General tally multiplier support has been added to the TallyManager.  Multiplier values are added to a vector stored in the TallyEvent that is independent of the list of tally observers (in the future it may be better to use an unordered map from the C++11 standard).  These values are accessed by a multiplier ID (i.e. vector index) that is stored in each TallyInput.  This allows different tallies to use the same multiplier ID without having to store/update it twice per event.  The tallies can then access this multiplier value in their compute_score methods using TallyEvent::get_score_multiplier, which returns the current particle_weight \* multiplier value (or just particle_weight if multiplier_id is not valid).

In DAG-MCNP, the multiplier ID is related to the fmesh index.  If no multipliers are used, then none are added to TallyManager.  However, the TallyManager::updateMultiplier method is currently still called for these tallies from MCNP even though it doesn't do anything.  This is how the original tally multiplier implementation worked for DAGMC tallies as it called dagmc_mesh_score every time, whether or not multipliers were used.  As a future performance improvement, if needed, the fmesh tallies that actually have multipliers can be stored in an array so that we only update the ones that need to be updated.  Alternatively, we could use a new DAGMC tally card instead of the existing FMESH tally card.

Contents of a batlab run-spec
After the remote_pre_declare call to a build script there is a remote_declare call to generate test names, followed by a remote_task call to run the test.  Typically it looks like
    • platform_name_remote_pre_declare build.sh
    • remote_declare generate_test_list.sh
    • remote_task run_test.sh

Generate_test_list.sh 

Build.sh builds the executables in whatever tree exists below the top-level CMakeLists.txt
In the cyclus application, generate_test_list.sh checks for the existence of the test executable, cyclus_unit_tests,  and calls
install/cyclus/bin/cyclus_unit_tests --gtest_list_tests  | python gen_test_list.py CYCLUS.
install/cyclus/bin/cyclus_unit_tests --gtest_list_tests  | python gen_test_list.py CYCLUS. > tasklist.nmi

Cyclus_unit_tests (it will be renamed to fludag_unit_tests for FluDAG) links the gtest-provided main with the compiled test files.  Although it has been renamed to something like cyclus_unit_test_driver.cc, it is really just gtest_main.cc, and brings along with it the ability to read some switches, including --gtest_list_test.  This lists all the individual tests, which are then piped to the python gen_test_list script.

Gen_test_list.py
This script lives in batlab.  It puts a word in front of each major and minor test and sends it to tasklist.nmi

> fludag_unit_tests --gtest_list_tests | python ../../tests/gen_test_list.py  FLUDAG.

```
$FLUPRO/flutil/rfluka -N0 -M${number} -e /path/to/mainfludag 
 -d <h5m filename> <inputfilename>
```

Where ${number} is the number of batches you would like for the calculation
            <h5m filename> is the full path to the appropriately tagged geometry file
            <input filename> is Fluka input file

The Fluka input file is where you control the number of particles to launch and other run time options.

My opinion is that a diff of the source code would probably not provide much insight. The reasons for this are:
1. MCNP6 has a vastly larger number of source files than MCNP5. MCNP5 has 336 source files whereas MCNP6 has 923. (If we only consider files in the `src` directory, MCNP6 has 490.)
2. There are a lot of whitespace changes. MCNP5 did not enforce a strict indent width, switching from 2 to 3 seemingly at random. MCNP6 uses 2 spaces everywhere.
3. Many variable names have changed. For example, the position varialbes in MCNP5 are `xxx`, `yyy`, and `zzz`, while in MCNP6, all the particle state information is stored in the `pbl` structure, and the position variables are `pbl%r%x`, `pbl%r%y`, and `pbl%r%z`.

That being said, it is usually possible to open up the same source files in MCNP5 and MCNP6 and figure out which portions of the code correspond. Most of the MCNP5 code affected by the DAGMC patch looks very similar to the same portions of the MCNP6 code.

Here are some of the biggest differences between the portions of MCNP5 affected by DAGMC and their MCNP6 counterparts:

The code handling the MPI calls has been completely rewritten for MCNP6. MCNP5 contains a `dotcomm` directory containing all the MPI subroutines, which are called from `msgcon.F90` and `msgtsk.F90`. MCNP6 does not contain that directory; instead, all the MPI subroutines were written from scratch and added to `messages.F90`.

There have been changes in MCNP's process for reading the input file. MCNP5 reads it twice: first in `pass1.F90` and second in `rdprob.F90`. MCNP6 reads it three times: first in `pass0.F90`, second in `pass1.F90`, and third in `rdprob.F90`. It turns out that the changes made to the MCNP5 version of `pass1.F90` should actually be applied to the MCNP6 version of `pass0.F90`, not `pass1.F90.`

The files `getpar.F90` and `savpar.F90` no longer exist in MCNP6; instead, their subroutines have been incorporated into `pblcom.F90`.

My main approach has been to go through the DAGMC patch for MCNP5, open up the relevant sections of the MCNP6 code, and incorporate the changes made in MCNP5 into MCNP6. This is a straightforward process when the code hasn't changed much between the versions, which is the case most of the time. It becomes more difficult when significant changes have occurred between the versions.

The biggest challenge will be integrating DAGMC into the features in MCNP6 not present in MCNP5, such as magnetic field tracking.

My current workflow has been run all the MCNP6 test problems (of which there are 1594) through mcnp2cad, editing the input files to match the new cell and surface numbers, and making sure they run properly. This is an arduous process.

So far I haven't experienced any major problems outside of the suite containing the problems with magnetic fields.

From [here](http://docencia.ac.upc.edu/FIB/USO/Bibliografia/unix-c-libraries.html)

Static Linking Vs. Dynamic Linking
----------------------------------------------------

When we discussed static libraries we said that the linker will try to look for a file named 'libutil.a'. We lied. Before looking for such a file, it will look for a file named 'libutil.so' - as a shared library. Only if it cannot find a shared library, will it look for 'libutil.a' as a static library. Thus, if we have created two copies of the library, one static and one shared, the shared will be preferred. This can be overridden using some linker flags ('-Wl,static' with some linkers, '-Bstatic' with other types of linkers. refer to the compiler's or the linker's manual for info about these flags).
I haven't combed through the CMake to check if we set this preference, but it's possible(likely?) that we could be linking to the shared MOAB libs even if the static ones are present.

After a little investigating, I've found that the CMake convention for supporting `<packagename>_ROOT` variables in `find_package` is relatively new, and that a user-defined variable `MOAB_ROOT` may be ignored in older versions of CMake, causing some existing  (more info [here](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/git-stage/policy/CMP0074.html)).

I think that policy related to `find_packages` (CMP0074) needs to be set in newer versions of CMake where it didn't need to be before?

Ah, I think I see what's going on here. In cmake 3.12+, `<package_name>_ROOT` variables are supposed to be intrinsic variables used by `find_package()` and are not meant to be used directly.

So perhaps it would be better to go back to using `MOAB_DIR` instead of `MOAB_ROOT`, because cmake doesn't assign any special meaning to `<package_name>_DIR` variables.

The only problem there is that they use the variable `MOAB_DIR` in their `MOABConfig.cmake`. This was causing problems, and is why I wanted to get ahead of this change. I think we can still use `MOAB_ROOT` we just have to enable this policy for CMake to support it. I'm verifying this on OpenMC's CI right now and will get back to you.

This seems to make the warning go away (and have it still work in versions of cmake that don't know what CMP0074 is):

```
if (CMAKE_VERSION VERSION_GREATER 3.11)
  cmake_policy(SET CMP0074 OLD)
endif ()
```
CMP is short for "CMake Policy". This particular policy defines the behavior of `find_package` with respect to our `*_ROOT` variables. I linked the formal description of the policy above.

    /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libm.a
```

Exported targets are a little different than the configuration file. CMake handles these automatically. When targets are exported, their linker, compiler, etc. info is all included in a file that, in this case, would be something like `MOABTargets.cmake`. Then in other packages relying on moab, this target file gets included as part of the `FindMOAB.cmake` and then targets can be used as though they were created as part of any projects that file is included into, in this case, DAGMC.


```
find_package(MOAB REQUIRED) # MOABTargets.cmake included in this step
add_library(dagmc <dagmc_sources>)
target_link_library(dagmc MOAB)
```

I am working on a PR (currently just a branch) that reverses the precedence of EIGEN and LAPACK in `Matrix3.hpp`.  Currently, as I see it, MOAB's HYPRE tool requires Eigen3, but the option to use LAPACK was introduced in `Matrix3`.

In the current code, using the precedence that Andy correctly indicates, you cannot use Eigen in HYPRE and LAPACK in Matrix3.  Rather, you get Eigen everywhere or LAPACK without HYPRE.

My fix will allow the combination.

That said, I'm not sure what the rest of the MOAB team wants/prefers/expects!?!

If we assume only CMake builds with `ENABLE_BLASLAPACK=OFF` does this PR fix all our problems?

Yes. If we only build moab with cmake, and we disable blas/lapack, then this PR should work.

The way the PR is set up right now is that if `MOAB_USE_LAPACK` evaluates to true (i.e. it is `ON` or `yes`), then it assumes moab is linked to lapack. If it evaluates to false (i.e. it is `OFF`, `no`, or empty), then it assumes moab is not linked to lapack.

The only situation I've been able to find where this PR would _not_ work is if you use moab 5.1.0, enable blas/lapack, have eigen present on the system, and use the cmake build. In this specific case, `MOAB_USE_LAPACK` will be set to `ON`, but moab will not be linked to lapack.

In every other case I tested, the value of `MOAB_USE_LAPACK` is set correctly depending on whether or not moab is linked to lapack.

My opinion is that it's handy to use in the right situations, but should be used cautiously. In certain situations it makes the code less verbose and more readable. Here I felt using it to replace the very long type definitions was worth it. I do try to avoid using it in places where the compiler will infer a type as that can lead to unexpected problems however. Using it as the return type in function signatures is one such example.

My only objection is the obfuscation it can cause with multi-header types, but that lack of clarity is fixed by an ide with type discovery.
